content:
Prices are rising. The CPI ticked up this quarter in a way that made economists uncomfortable, though the discomfort came wrapped in the careful language they use when they're worried and not yet willing to say so. Transitory, they said. Supply chain disruptions. Base effects. Temporary pressures that will resolve as the pandemic recedes and normality returns.

Transitory. I want to remember that word, because I suspect it will define this era's monetary misjudgement the way irrational exuberance defined the last one.

Here's what I actually observe. Energy costs are rising, and the constraints producing them aren't temporary - they're structural: underinvestment in production, regulatory barriers to new capacity, and a geopolitical reshuffling that is turning energy into a weapon. Food costs are rising, driven by those same energy costs feeding into fertiliser, transport, processing and cold storage. Shipping costs remain elevated because the container fleet wasn't built for a pandemic recovery and can't be expanded on the timeline the recovery demands. Labour costs are rising because the pandemic reshuffled the workforce in ways that created shortages in sectors that can't automate fast enough to compensate.

None of these are transitory. Each reflects a structural shift that will take years rather than months to work through. And the people calling it transitory are working from a framework calibrated for a world that has stopped existing, which is a more troubling problem than dishonesty and a much harder one to correct.

**A Generation That Has Never Seen It**

I keep coming back to institutional memory, because I think its absence explains more here than any of the models do.

The people currently running the Reserve Bank, the Federal Reserve, the Bank of England and the ECB - the people setting rates and money supply and deciding how to respond to rising prices - are overwhelmingly people who built their careers during the great disinflation. From the early 1990s through 2020, inflation across the developed world was low, stable and falling. An entire generation of central bankers, economists, treasury officials and financial professionals came of age in a world where inflation simply wasn't the problem.

This isn't a small thing. Professional judgement is shaped by experience, and when the experience is thirty years of falling inflation, judgement tends towards complacency about the possibility of rising inflation. The models were trained on disinflationary data. The intuitions formed under disinflationary conditions. The institutional culture was optimised for a world where the risk was deflation and where the correct response to any stress was to cut rates and print money.

These are capable people confronting something their careers never prepared them for, and institutions staffed by people who have never navigated a thing tend to navigate it badly. Not through stupidity. Through the ordinary human difficulty of recognising a situation you have no template for while it's still early enough to matter.

**Who Actually Pays**

The distributional side is what troubles me most, and it gets the least attention.

Inflation tends to be discussed as though it were uniform - prices rise, everyone pays more, the economy adjusts. That's misleading. Inflation is distributive. It takes from some people and gives to others, and the pattern of taking and giving is anything but random.

It helps debtors and hurts creditors, because debts are denominated in nominal terms. If you owe 500,000 dollars on a mortgage and inflation erodes the real value of that debt, you benefit and the bank loses. Which means homeowners with large mortgages are, perversely, beneficiaries of moderate inflation.

The people who suffer are at the other end. People on fixed incomes whose payments don't adjust. People holding cash savings that quietly lose purchasing power. People whose wages lag prices because their bargaining position is weak. Renters, whose housing costs rise with the market while their incomes don't.

Inflation is a regressive tax that nobody voted for. It falls hardest on those least able to bear it and least equipped to hedge against it. The wealthy hold assets - property, equities, commodities - that rise with it. The poor hold cash that falls. The gap widens, and it widens without any minister having to announce anything.

The historical record here isn't ambiguous. Every significant inflation of the twentieth century came with widening inequality, deteriorating social trust and political instability. Weimar is the extreme case, but the pattern holds at far lower levels. When prices outrun wages, people conclude - correctly - that the system is failing them. They then look for explanations, and the explanations they find aren't always accurate, though they're always powerful.

I want to be clear that hyperinflation isn't my prediction and catastrophe isn't my prediction. What I expect is narrower and more likely: that this inflation proves considerably less transitory than the institutions managing it believe, and that the response arrives slower and weaker than it needs to, because the decision-makers have never made these decisions before, and because the institutional incentive is always to hope a problem resolves itself rather than act early and risk being wrong in public.

If I could change one thing, it would be to make the delay itself visible. Central banks publish forecasts and minutes; they don't publish how long it took them to act after their own indicators crossed a threshold. A simple published lag - indicator breached on this date, action taken on that one - would put a cost on hesitation that currently has none. Institutions respond to what gets measured about them, and right now nothing measures the thing most likely to go wrong.

From Adelaide, watching the supermarket prices tick up week by week, the word that keeps occurring to me is unfamiliar. Transitory implies we know the shape of the thing and are waiting for it to pass, and we don't know the shape of this. The institutions tasked with responding are meeting something they have no template for, unfamiliarity produces hesitation, and hesitation in the face of rising prices produces exactly the delay that lets the rise entrench.

Inflation is an experience long before it becomes a number, and the people deciding what to do about it have never had the experience. That gap - between the decision-makers and the reality they're managing - is the thing I'd watch most closely over the next two years.
